title: Polynomial algebras over Noetherian Cohen–Macaulay rings are Cohen–Macaulay
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] such that for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$, its local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] satisfies $\operatorname{depth}(R_{\mathfrak p})=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$, where depth is as in [def-weil-pbc-depth] and Krull dimension as in [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. For every integer $n\ge0$, the polynomial ring $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] is Noetherian and for every prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset P$ one has $\operatorname{depth}(P_{\mathfrak q})=\dim P_{\mathfrak q}$. Thus every finite-variable polynomial algebra over $R$ is Cohen–Macaulay, with that term meaning the displayed equality at all prime localizations.

proof.text: Use the finite-variable Noetherian instance for `S = MvPolynomial (Fin n) R`. The canonical algebra map R → S is flat because S is free over R.

source.place: finite multivariate polynomial algebra and free-module flatness

proof.text: For a prime q of S, contract it to p in R. The prime-spectrum fibre equivalence gives a prime Q of p.Fiber S and identifies the contraction of Q with q.
Apply the flat-fibre depth and height formulas to p and Q. They express depth(S_q) and height(q) as the sums of the corresponding base and fibre terms.

The fibre p.Fiber S is ring-equivalent to a finite multivariate polynomial ring over the residue field. The polynomial regular-ring theorem therefore supplies IsRegularRing for the fibre, and hence IsRegularLocalRing for its prime localization.

For a regular local ring, choose a finite list generating the maximal ideal. The regular-system-of-parameters theorem makes this list regular, giving depth at least its span dimension; the depth-support-dimension theorem gives the reverse inequality. Thus depth equals Krull dimension.

Use hCM for the base localization and the preceding regular-local equality for the fibre localization. Rewrite both heights as localization dimensions and substitute into the depth formula; the two sums agree, proving the assertion for q.
